section.content: A machine learning system for processing data corresponding to an incoming transaction. The machine learning system includes a classification history module including a memory configured to store status data for a plurality of categories indexed by respective category identifiers, wherein the status data stored in the memory for each category identifier corresponds to previous transactions associated with the entity and the respective category. The decay logic is configured to modify the state data stored in the memory based on a time difference between a time of an incoming transaction and a time of a previous transaction. When the memory contains state data for an entity and category identifier pair associated with an incoming transaction, a time-difference dependent decay function is applied to the stored state data to generate a decay version. The state data output from the decay logic stage is updated using an input tensor generated from data corresponding to the incoming transaction to generate updated state data.

用于处理与到来的交易对应的数据的机器学习系统。机器学习系统包括分类历史模块，分类历史模块包括：存储器，其被配置成存储由相应的类别标识符索引的多个类别的状态数据，其中在存储器中针对每个类别标识符存储的状态数据对应于与实体和相应的类别相关联的先前交易。衰减逻辑级被配置成基于到来的交易的时间与先前交易的时间之间的时间差来修改存储在存储器中的状态数据。当存储器包含与到来的交易相关联的实体和类别标识符对的状态数据时，将依赖于时间差的衰减函数应用于所存储的状态数据以生成衰减版本。使用根据与到来的交易对应的数据生成的输入张量来更新从衰减逻辑级输出的状态数据，以生成更新的状态数据。

Machine learning systemTechnical Field

The present invention relates to a classification history module (categorical history module) for a machine learning system, in particular for use in a machine learning system that detects anomalies in patterns of data, such as detection of fraudulent transactions. Certain examples relate to machine learning systems for use in real-time transaction processing.

Background

Over the last two decades digital payments have evolved dramatically, with over three-quarters of global payments using some form of payment card or electronic wallet. Point-of-sale systems are becoming digitized instead of cash-based. In short, global business systems now rely heavily on electronic data processing platforms. This presents a number of engineering challenges that are not primarily faced by ordinary (lay) users. For example, digital transactions need to be completed in real-time, i.e., the computer device experiences a minimum level of delay in purchasing. Digital transactions also need to be secure and resistant to attacks and exploitation. The processing of digital transactions is also limited by the historical development of global electronic payment systems. For example, many infrastructures remain configured around models designed for main framework architectures used more than 50 years ago.

As digital transactions increase, new security risks become apparent. Digital transactions present new opportunities for fraud and malicious activity. In 2015, it was estimated that 7% of digital transactions were fraudulent and that this number only increased as economic activity transitioned over more lines. Fraud losses are estimated to be four times (e.g., in dollars) the world population and are also growing.

As traditional fraud prevention methods such as identity authentication (e.g., passwords, digital biometrics, national IDs, etc.) have proven ineffective in preventing fraudulent carriers such as synthetic identities and fraud, financial services institutions are being more scrutinized. These much more complex fraud threat carriers require a large number of more analyses in a very short (less than 50 ms) time and are typically based on the data sample size being much smaller for fraud or fraud itself. This presents a significant technical challenge.

While the risk of fraud and the like is an economic issue for companies participating in commerce, implementation of the technical system for processing transactions is an engineering challenge. Traditionally, banks, merchants, and card issuers developed "paper" rules or programs that were manually implemented by clerks to mark or block certain transactions. As transactions become digitized, one way to build a technical system for processing transactions is to provide a set of these developed standards to computer engineers and require them to be implemented using a digital representation of the transaction, i.e., converting handwritten rules into coded logical statements that can be applied to electronic transaction data. As the amount of digital transactions grows, this conventional approach encounters several problems. First, the processing of any application needs to be done "in real time", e.g. with a millisecond delay. Second, thousands of transactions per second need to be processed (e.g., a common "load" may be 1000 to 2000 per second), where the load may change unexpectedly over time (e.g., the issuance of a new product or set of tickets may easily increase the average load level by a factor of several). Third, for security reasons, the transaction processor and the bank's digital storage system are typically isolated or partitioned, whereas digital transactions typically involve an interconnected network of business systems. Fourth, large-scale analysis of actual reported fraud and predicted fraud is now possible. The method shows that the traditional fraud detection method has the defects of low accuracy and high false alarm rate. This will have a physical impact on the digital transaction process, more real point-of-sale and online purchases are denied, and those attempting to utilize the new digital system will typically go beyond the ease.

More machine learning methods have been employed for processing transaction data over the past few years. As machine learning models mature in academia, engineers have begun to attempt to apply them to the processing of transactional data. However, this again encounters a problem. Even if an engineer is provided with an academic or theoretical machine learning model and is required to implement it, this is not simple. For example, large-scale transaction processing systems begin to present problems. Machine learning models do not have the luxury of having unlimited reasoning time as in the laboratory. This means that it is not practical at all to implement certain models in a real-time environment, or that they require significant adjustments to allow real-time processing at the level experienced by real-world servers. Furthermore, engineers need to deal with the problem of implementing machine learning models on data that is isolated or partitioned based on access security, and in cases where the speed of data update is extremely fast. Thus, the problems faced by engineers constructing transaction processing systems may be considered similar to those faced by network or database engineers, requiring the application of a machine learning model, but meeting the system throughput and query response time constraints set by the processing infrastructure. These problems have no simple solution. In fact, many transaction processing systems are confidential, proprietary and based on the fact of old technology, meaning that engineers do not have a knowledge system developed in these adjacent domains and often face challenges specific to the transaction processing domain. Furthermore, the field of mass-utility machine learning remains inexperienced and there are few established design patterns or textbooks that engineers can rely on.

The fraud detection system generates a risk score for the new transaction in real time (i.e., delay < = 100 milliseconds), where a high risk score indicates the likelihood of fraud, errors, or unauthorized use of the account. The financial institution uses these scores in its decision logic in deciding whether to approve the transaction (typically, if the risk score is above a certain threshold, the transaction will be rejected). Financial institutions often want a collection of transactions above a certain risk threshold to contain as high a proportion of fraud as possible (i.e., provide a "highest detection rate") while the false positive classification rate is as low as possible (i.e., provide a "highest accuracy").

One approach known per se in the art involves the use of machine learning techniques such as Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to detect anomalies in patterns of behavior. Those skilled in the art will appreciate that the output of the RNN is the next state and that this next state depends on the previous state and the inputs provided to the RNN. In this way, the state of the RNN is based not only on transient information related to a given transaction, but also on the history of transactions that have previously occurred, thus preserving the memory of patterns that have been observed. This may be used to detect abnormal behavior that may be indicative of fraudulent transactions. The terms "behavior" and "behavioral" are used herein to refer to a pattern of activity or action.

Such detection of abnormal activity may provide an improvement in the security of the system when compared to "traditional" fraud prevention methods (e.g., passwords, digital biometrics, country IDs, etc.). Of course, it will be appreciated that behavior pattern analysis techniques may be suitably employed in conjunction with one or more of these "traditional" approaches.

In general, a given machine learning system may be configured to process transactions involving many different entities (e.g., different cardholders). The behavior patterns of each entity may be different and typically the history of each entity must be kept independently in order to detect abnormal behavior for that entity. Thus, machine learning systems for high volume transaction processing pipelines typically store state data for each entity (i.e., cardholder).

Applicants have appreciated that the duration between successive transactions for a given entity may vary, typically significantly. Thus, the previous state should have a degree of impact in determining the legitimacy of the new transaction. The applicant's prior patent applications, published as WO/2022/008130 and WO/2022/008131, each of which is incorporated herein by reference, describe an arrangement in which the status data of a given entity decays based on the period of time that has elapsed since the status data was stored (i.e. since the last transaction of the entity).

Data scientists who build machine learning models typically expend a great deal of effort to design models and extract machine learning features for these models, resulting in an optimal tradeoff between detection rate and accuracy.

However, the applicant has appreciated that further improvements may be made to the technical system in which the correlation analysis is performed. In particular, applicants have recognized that the novelty of the interaction of entities (e.g., the novelty of the relationship between an account holder and a particular merchant) is useful in detecting anomalous behavior. The novelty of buyer-seller interactions is an important signal to maximize the performance of these scores. The established relationship is a good indication that the new activity is authentic (i.e., performed honest by the buyer), while the novel relationship indicates greater suspicion of the new activity (which may generally be considered in connection with other risk signals).

The present invention seeks to provide improvements to machine learning systems to automatically extract novelty such as interactions between buyers and sellers.

Disclosure of Invention

According to a first aspect, embodiments of the present invention provide a machine learning system for processing data corresponding to an incoming transaction associated with an entity, the machine learning system comprising a classification history module (categorical history module) configured to process at least some of the data, the classification history module comprising:

i) A memory configured to store status data for a plurality of categories indexed by respective category identifiers, wherein the status data stored in the memory for each category identifier corresponds to previous transactions associated with the entity and the respective category;

ii) a decay logic stage configured to modify state data stored in the memory based on a time difference between a time of an incoming transaction (incoming transaction) and a time of a previous transaction, the decay logic stage configured to:

a) When the memory contains state data of an entity and category identifier pair (ENTITY AND category IDENTIFIER PAIR) associated with an incoming transaction, retrieving the state data and applying a decay function to the state data to generate a decayed version of the state data, wherein the decay function is time-difference dependent and outputs a decayed version of the state data, and

Iii) An update logic stage configured to update state data output from the decay logic stage using an input tensor generated from data corresponding to an incoming transaction to generate updated state data, store the updated state data in memory for an entity and category identifier pair associated with the incoming transaction, and output an output tensor comprising the updated state data;

iv) wherein the machine learning system is configured to map the output tensor from the classification history module to a scalar value representing the likelihood that the incoming transaction presents an anomaly within the sequence of actions, and

V) wherein the scalar value is used to determine whether to approve or reject the incoming transaction.

It will thus be appreciated that embodiments of the present invention provide an improved arrangement in which state data relating to previous transactions of a matched category is stored in memory and the stored state data of a given category is retrieved the next time there is a transaction for the same entity that matches the given category (i.e. for the pair of entity and category identifier associated with the newly incoming transaction). Categories that may be used are described in further detail below, however, in general, categories may include, for example, merchants, merchant types, transaction amounts, time of day, or some combination of these.

Thus, the classification history module provides a mechanism for tracking patterns of transactions across specific categories. Unlike conventional mechanisms such as a time decay unit that typically retrieves a state from a previous transaction (i.e., an immediately preceding transaction of the entity), the classification history module selectively retrieves state data corresponding to the same category as the current transaction, which may not be the most recent transaction, and may have elapsed a significant period of time since the previous transaction of that category was processed, during which any number of intermediate transactions corresponding to other categories occurred simultaneously. This allows extracting a signal providing information about the novelty of the interaction between an entity and a particular category, wherein such novelty, or a pattern of behavior related to the novelty, may be indicative of abnormal behavior (e.g. fraud).

Advantageously, embodiments of the present invention may provide significant improvements in speed and/or confidentiality of the implementation. In particular, data scientists no longer need to manually design this type of features, meaning that they do not need to be disclosed as input to a classifier for model management, and the implementation time of the model may be reduced.

Embodiments of the present invention may also advantageously provide improvements in detection performance. The classification history module may learn more subtle interaction logic than a human being would manually design in a limited time. In particular, the classification history module may learn that only certain types of activities qualify as trust builds that score the current type of activity. Applicants have found that the use of the present invention generally translates into a significant detection enhancement over methods that may be known per se in the art.

Embodiments of the present invention may be applied to a variety of digital transactions including, but not limited to, card payments, so-called "wire transfer" transfers, point-to-point payments, automated clearing system (BACS) payments for banks, and Automated Clearing House (ACH) payments. The output of the machine learning system may be used to prevent various fraud and criminals, such as card fraud, application fraud, payment fraud, merchant fraud, game fraud, and money laundering.

As outlined above, the classification history module retrieves status data corresponding to the same category as the incoming transaction. Typically, the memory may store status data for each possible category (e.g., each merchant or each merchant type), however in practice this may not be the case. For example, a limit may be placed on the number of categories of state data that may be stored in memory. This may be due to hardware or software limitations of a given implementation, or may be a design decision that limits the amount of state data that is retained to some particular amount. Thus, it is possible that an incoming transaction may correspond to a category for which no existing state data for the corresponding category identifier stored in memory exists at this time. In some implementations, the attenuation logic stage is further configured to:

When the memory does not contain state data for the entity and category identifier pair associated with the incoming transaction, new state data is generated and output. For example, the new state data may typically include a zero tensor—however, it will be appreciated that some other default tensor may be used for the new state data, if appropriate.

In general, data from an incoming transaction may be converted into an input tensor suitable for input to the rest of the machine learning system. Those skilled in the art will appreciate that the input tensor may be considered a feature tensor or vector, i.e., a tensor of values, where each value corresponds to the extent to which an incoming transaction has certain features. In some implementations, the machine learning system further includes a first neural network stage configured to apply a neural network layer having a respective plurality of learned weights to data corresponding to the incoming transactions to generate an input tensor, and to provide the input tensor to an update logic stage of the classification history module. In other words, the first neural network may be described as an embedded layer. In some embodiments, the first neural network may include a first multi-layer perceptron (MLP).

Similarly, the output tensor generated by the update logic stage is mapped to a scalar value, as outlined above. In some implementations, the machine learning system further includes a second neural network stage configured to apply a second neural network layer having a corresponding plurality of learned weights to the output tensor generated by the update logic stage of the classification history module to generate a scalar value representative of a likelihood that the incoming transaction presents an anomaly within the sequence of actions. In some implementations, the second neural network may include a second multi-layer perceptron (MLP).

Those skilled in the art will appreciate that an MLP is a feed-forward neural network that is generally constructed from at least an input layer, a hidden layer, and an output layer, where each layer includes a plurality of nodes. The hidden layer and output layer nodes have an activation function (e.g., a nonlinear activation function). The nodes from each layer are connected to the nodes in the subsequent layer with a certain weight (typically each node in one layer is connected to each node in the next layer). These weights may be learned during a training phase (e.g., during supervised learning), such as via back propagation.

In some implementations, the update logic stage includes a third neural network stage configured to generate updated state data using the attenuated state data and an input tensor derived from the incoming transaction. In other words, updated state data may also be generated by the neural network layer. The neural network layer may also use trained weights. In some embodiments, the third neural network stage may include a recurrent neural network.

The amount of time that passes between successive transactions of a given entity (e.g., cardholder) belonging to a particular category may vary significantly. For example, if a category includes merchant identities and status data is stored for each merchant (i.e., status data from previous buyer-seller interactions involving the card holder and merchant), it may occur that the card may be used several times a week by one merchant while the same card may be spaced weeks or months between transactions by another merchant. Similarly, different entities may have transactions conducted at very different rates, and the behavior patterns of any given entity may change over time.

It is understood that when determining the legitimacy of a new incoming transaction, the amount of time that has passed since the relevant status data retrieved from memory for a particular entity and category combination of the incoming transaction was stored may have a significant impact on its relevance. The decay logic stage modifies the state data to reduce its effect.

The decay function is used to reduce the effect of previous state data based on its degree of aging. In one set of embodiments, the decay logic is configured to modify the status data of the entity associated with the incoming transaction stored in the memory based on a time difference between a time of the incoming transaction and a time of a most recent transaction of the entity. In other words, in such an embodiment, the entire state data table of the entity is attenuated each time there is a transaction for the entity. Advantageously, the method does not require any record keeping of the time each category of the entity was last seen, but rather uses a single timestamp for each entity, where the timestamp corresponds to the last transaction of the entity (whichever category the transaction relates to). In some such embodiments, the memory is configured to store a timestamp of the state data stored in the memory for each entity. Attenuating the state tables of a particular entity may advantageously reduce latency (as compared to attenuating tables of all entities) while eliminating the need to store a timestamp for each entity-class pair (as in the case of attenuating only state data of a particular entity-class pair, as outlined below with respect to a set of alternative embodiments).

In an alternative set of embodiments, the decay logic is configured to modify all state data of each entity stored in the memory based on a time difference between a time of an incoming transaction and a time of an immediately preceding transaction. In other words, in such an embodiment, each time a transaction exists, the entire state data table for all entities is decayed using the timestamp associated with the last transaction (whichever the transaction relates to), regardless of which entity the transaction is directed to. However, it will be appreciated that this may entail significant computational requirements to mitigate unnecessary delay increases.

In another set of alternative embodiments, the decay logic stage is configured to modify only state data stored in memory for an entity and category identifier pair associated with an incoming transaction, wherein the decay logic stage modifies the state data based on a time difference between a time of the incoming transaction and a time of a previous transaction of the entity and category identifier pair associated with the incoming transaction. Under this arrangement, only the status data of a particular entity and category combination is attenuated each time there is a transaction for that combination. In some such embodiments, the memory is configured to store a timestamp of each state data stored in the memory. The time stamp may form part of the status data or may be stored separately. Advantageously, the method does not require the entire table to be decayed every transaction, which may enable faster processing under the trade-off of increasing memory usage to store the time stamps.

There are a number of options for implementing the storage of state data in memory. However, in some implementations, the memory is configured as a stack such that the retrieved state data is removed from the stack and such that updated state data is stored at the top of the stack. According to such an embodiment, the most recent entity-category interactions may be at the top of the stack, while the least recent interactions are at the bottom of the stack.

In some implementations, the classification history module is configured such that when the memory is full, the stored state data for the at least one class identifier is erased. In some such embodiments, the classification history module is configured such that when the memory is full, the stored state data for the least recently seen class identifier is erased. Under such an arrangement, the oldest data is "discarded" from memory to make room for the new data. In practice, this provides an additional "forget" function, in which too old data is removed, provided that the memory size is properly selected. In general, the size of the memory may be selected to ensure that the data desired to be retained is not conventionally erased from the memory.

In some implementations, the state data stored for each entity and category identifier pair includes a tensor of values. Each value in the tensor may correspond to some feature or combination of features that the transaction may have, with the magnitude of the value providing a measure of the strength with which the transaction (or pattern of previous transactions) exhibits such features.

In some such embodiments, the decay function applies a respective decay multiplier (e.g., exponential decay) to each of the values. It will be appreciated that a different multiplier (e.g., a different exponential decay) may be applied to each value. The use of different decay multipliers for different values enables the strength of the memory to be set differently for different features. It may be desirable that the history of certain features remain for a longer period of time than other features. For example, the status data may relate to (i.e., depend on) an average transaction amount for transactions of the entity and category identifier pair, and it may be useful to maintain the impact of the average for months (e.g., 6 months or 12 months) at a time. At the same time, status data that is dependent on transaction speed (i.e. transaction rate per unit time) may be of interest in a shorter period of time (e.g. during 1 or 2 hours), and thus may preferably limit its impact outside such a period of time. It will be appreciated that in practice, the values stored in the state data may not have a direct (i.e., one-to-one) correspondence with any one or more particular features, but rather each value is a function of one or more features. In other words, the values generated (e.g., via a neural network layer) are stored as state data, and each value may have complex dependencies on multiple features. The relationship between these features and the corresponding state data values (i.e., numerical values) attributed thereto may be learned during training. Thus, it should be appreciated that there need not be any user-specified attenuation of state data associated with any particular feature, but rather that the machine learning system may learn that historical state data derived from certain features (such as the previously described examples) or combinations of such features should be retained longer than other data.

The decay multiplier may be appropriately selected to tailor the memory retention level appropriately for each feature. In at least some embodiments, these decay multipliers may be predetermined, i.e., they may be preset. According to some such embodiments, the machine learning system may learn that values derived from certain features or combinations of features should be subjected to one or more of these decay factors to varying degrees, i.e., the decay factors affect the end-to-end training process.

However, in some embodiments, at least some (and possibly all) of the decay multipliers may be learned. Instead of pre-providing a choice of attenuation factors, the machine learning system can learn by itself the best attenuation factors to use and what state data those learned attenuation factors should be for.

In general, the decay multipliers may be arranged as tensors (or vectors, etc.) such that the temporal decay may be multiplied element-by-element with the state data to be decayed. In the case where classification status data is stored in a table and each column in the table may be indexed by a class identifier, a tensor of time decay (or vector, etc.) may be multiplied element by element with each column of the table. It will of course be appreciated that the table could equivalently be configured such that the status data is stored in the row indexed by the category identifier.

As outlined above, the classification history module provides a pattern across transactions for particular entity and category pairs to be retained. In some implementations, the machine learning system further includes a time decay unit module configured to process at least some of the data corresponding to the incoming transaction, the time decay unit module including:

A second memory configured to store second status data corresponding to an immediately preceding transaction, and

A second decay logic stage configured to modify the second state data stored in the second memory based on a time difference between a time of an incoming transaction and a time of an immediately preceding transaction. Those skilled in the art will appreciate that unlike the classification history module, the time decay unit module functions on a transaction-by-transaction basis for a particular entity, regardless of the class to which the transactions relate.

According to such embodiments, the classification history module and the time decay unit module may be arranged in parallel with each other and provide complementary analysis of incoming transactions. The classification history module facilitates detection of anomalies (e.g., fraud) based on novelty in interactions between an entity (e.g., cardholder) and a category (e.g., merchant type, time of day, transaction amount, etc.), while the time decay unit module facilitates detection of anomalies based on recent transaction behavior of the entity in all categories.

In some such embodiments, wherein the time decay unit module further comprises:

A fourth neural network stage configured to determine next state data using the previous state data modified by the second decay logic stage and a second input tensor derived from the incoming transaction, the fourth neural network stage configured to store the next state data in the second memory. In some embodiments, the fourth neural network stage may include a recurrent neural network.

In embodiments that provide both a classification history module and a time decay unit, data corresponding to an incoming transaction is provided to each of the classification history module and the time decay unit. Each of these modules may receive different data, or there may be some (or possibly complete) overlap in the data received by each module. In general, it is contemplated that two modules will act on different features, and thus the data provided to each module may be specific to the respective module.

In the case of generating an input tensor from an incoming transaction using a neural network layer (e.g., MLP) with learned weights, the same neural network layer may generate the input tensor such that a first portion of the input tensor is provided to the classification history module and a second portion of the input tensor is provided to the time decay unit module.

In some embodiments using time-decay unit modules, the machine learning system is configured to map output data from both the time-decay unit module and the classification history module to scalar values representing the likelihood that an incoming transaction presents an anomaly within the sequence of actions.

In some implementations, the memory is configured to store status data for a plurality of entities, wherein for each entity, a plurality of categories indexed by a respective category identifier are stored, wherein the status data stored in the memory for each category identifier corresponds to previous transactions associated with the respective entity and the respective category.

It will be appreciated that references herein to "category" relate to some aspect of a transaction, that is, a category may be considered as a group or tag that may be applied to transactions that meet some criteria. For example, a category may represent an entity (or "primary" entity, which may be, for example, a cardholder) with which a different secondary entity (e.g., a merchant) transacts. Many different categories may be used. In some implementations, each of the plurality of categories includes one or more of a secondary entity, a secondary entity type, a transaction value interval (transaction value band), a day of the week, a time of day, an hour of day, and a time window. In a particular set of embodiments, the plurality of categories may include a composite of one or more of the categories.

When viewed from a second aspect, embodiments of the present invention provide a method of processing data associated with a proposed transaction, the method comprising:

receiving an incoming event from a client transaction processing system, the incoming event being associated with a request for approval decisions for the proposed transaction;

parsing the incoming event to extract data for the proposed transaction, including determining a time difference between the proposed transaction and a prior transaction;

A machine learning system to apply embodiments of the first aspect of the present invention to output a scalar value representing a likelihood that a proposed transaction presents an anomaly within an action sequence based on the extracted data and time differences, the application comprising accessing a memory to retrieve at least state data for an entity and a category identifier associated with the transaction;

Determining a binary output based on scalar values output by the machine learning system, the binary output representing whether the proposed transaction is approved or rejected, and

The binary output is returned to the client transaction processing system.

A second aspect of the invention extends to a non-transitory computer readable medium comprising instructions that, when executed by a processor, cause the processor to perform a method of processing data associated with a proposed transaction, the method comprising:

Detailed Description

Certain example embodiments are described herein that relate to a machine learning system for use in transaction processing. In some implementations, a machine learning system is applied in a real-time, high-volume transaction processing pipeline to provide an indication of whether a transaction or entity matches a previously observed and/or predicted activity or action pattern, such as an indication of whether the transaction or entity is "normal" or "abnormal. The term "behavioral" as used herein refers to a pattern of such activity or action. The indication may include scalar values normalized within a predefined range (e.g., 0 to 1), which may then be used to prevent fraud and other abuse of the payment system. The machine learning system may apply a machine learning model that is updated as more transactional data is obtained, e.g., a machine learning model that is continually trained based on new data, to reduce false positives and maintain accuracy of the output metrics. This example may be particularly useful for preventing fraud in situations where the actual presence of a payment card cannot be determined (e.g., online transactions known as "card-less payments"), or commercial transactions where high value transactions may be conventional and it may be difficult to classify the behavior pattern as "unexpected". Thus, this example facilitates the processing of transactions where they are primarily "online", i.e., digitally conducted over one or more public communication networks.

Certain embodiments described herein enable machine learning models to be customized to a behavioral pattern between pairs of certain entities (such as account holders) and categories (such as merchants, transaction amounts, time of day, etc.). For example, a machine learning model may model entity-category-specific behavior patterns. The machine learning system described herein is capable of providing a dynamically updated machine learning model despite large transaction flows and/or despite the need to separate different data sources.

As previously outlined, embodiments of the present invention may be applied to a variety of digital transactions, including but not limited to card payments, so-called "wire transfer" transfers, point-to-point payments, automated clearing system (BACS) payments for banks, and Automated Clearing House (ACH) payments. The output of the machine learning system may be used to prevent various fraud and criminals, such as card fraud, application fraud, payment fraud, merchant fraud, game fraud, and money laundering.

The present exemplary machine learning system (e.g., configured and/or trained as outlined below) is configured to detect novelty in entity-category interactions.

Example transaction processing flow

Fig. 5A and 5B illustrate two possible transaction processing flows 500 and 550, respectively. These process flows may occur in the context of the example transaction processing systems 100, 102, 104 shown in fig. 1A-1C, as well as other systems. The process flows 500 and 550 are provided as one example of a context in which a machine learning transaction processing system may be applied, however, not all transaction process flows will necessarily follow the process shown in fig. 5A and 5B, and the process flows may vary between implementations, between systems, and over time. The example transaction processing flows 500 and 550 reflect two possible scenarios, a first scenario represented by the transaction processing flow 500, in which the transaction is approved, and a second scenario represented by the transaction processing flow 550, in which the transaction is rejected. Each transaction processing flow 500, 550 involves the same set of five interactive systems and devices, POS or user device 502, merchant system 504, payment Processor (PP) system 506, machine Learning (ML) system 508, and issuing bank system 510.POS or user device 502 may include one of client devices 110, merchant system 504 may include merchant server 130, payment processor system 506 may include payment processor server 140, and machine learning system 508 may include an implementation of machine learning systems 160, 210, and/or 402. The issuing bank system 510 may include one or more server devices that implement transaction functions on behalf of the issuing bank. The five interactive systems and devices 502-510 may be communicatively coupled via one or more internal or external communication channels, such as network 120. In some cases, some of these systems may be combined, for example, the issuing bank may also act as a payment processor, and thus systems 506 and 510 may be implemented with a common system. In other cases, similar process flows may be performed specifically for merchants (e.g., without involving a payment processor or issuing bank). In this case, the machine learning system 508 may communicate directly with the merchant system 504. In these variations, the general functional transaction processing flow may remain similar to the flow described below.

The transaction processing flow in both fig. 5A and 5B includes a plurality of common (i.e., shared) processes 512 through 528. At block 512, the POS or user device 502 initiates a transaction. For a POS device, this may include the cashier attempting to make an electronic payment using the front-end device, and for user device 502, this may include the user making an online purchase using a credit or debit card or an online payment account (e.g., clicking on "done" in an online shopping basket). At block 514, the payment details are received as electronic data by merchant system 504. At block 516, the transaction is processed by merchant system 504 and a request for authorizing a payment is made to payment processor system 506. At block 518, the payment processor system 506 receives the request from the merchant system 504. The request may be made through a proprietary communication channel or as a secure request over a public network (e.g., HTTPS request over the internet). The payment processor system 506 then requests a score or probability for processing the transaction from the machine learning system 508. Block 518 may also include retrieving the assistance data to combine with the transaction data sent to the machine learning system 508 as part of the request. In other cases, the machine learning system 508 may access a data storage device (e.g., similar to the configuration of fig. 2A and 2B) that stores the assistance data and, thus, retrieve the data as part of the internal operation (e.g., based on identifiers provided within the transaction data and/or as defined as part of the implemented machine learning model).

Block 520 illustrates model initialization operations that occur prior to any request from the payment processor system 506. For example, the model initialization operation may include loading a defined machine learning model and instantiating parameters of the defined machine learning model. At block 522, the machine learning system 508 receives a request from the payment processor system 506 (e.g., via a data input interface such as 412 in fig. 4). At block 522, the machine learning system 508 may perform any defined preprocessing prior to applying the machine learning model initialized at block 520. For example, where the transaction data still retains character data (such as a merchant identified by a character string or character transaction description), this may be converted into suitable structured digital data (e.g., by converting string classification data into identifiers via a lookup operation or other mapping, and/or by mapping characters or character groups into vector embeddings (vector embeddings)). Then, at block 524, the machine learning system 506 applies the instantiated machine learning model, supplying the model with input data derived from the received request. This may include applying a machine learning model platform 414 as described with reference to fig. 4. At block 526, a scalar output is generated from the instantiated machine learning model. This may be processed at the machine learning system 508 to determine an "approve" or "reject" binary decision or, preferably, returned to the payment processor system 506 as a response to the request made at block 518.

At block 528, the output of the machine learning system 508 is received by the payment processor system 506 and used to approve or reject the transaction. Fig. 5A illustrates a process of approving a transaction based on the output of the machine learning system 508, and fig. 5B illustrates a process of rejecting a transaction based on the output of the machine learning system 508. In FIG. 5A, at block 528, the transaction is approved. A request is then made to the issuing bank system 532 at block 530. At block 534, the issuing bank system 532 approves or denies the request. For example, if the end user or cardholder has sufficient funds and approval to pay for the transaction cost, the issuing bank system 532 may approve the request. In some cases, the issuing bank system 532 may apply a second level of security, however, this may not be necessary if the issuing bank relies on anomaly detection performed by the payment processor using the machine learning system 508. At block 536, authorization from the issuing bank system 510 is returned to the payment processor system 506, which in turn sends a response to the merchant system 504 at block 538, and the merchant system 504 in turn responds to the POS or user device 502 at block 540. If the issuing bank system 510 approves the transaction at block 534, the transaction may be completed and a positive response returned to the POS or user device 502 via merchant system 504. The end user may experience it as an "authorized" message on the screen of the POS or user device 502. Merchant system 504 may then complete the purchase (e.g., initiate an internal process to complete the purchase).

At a later point in time, one or more of merchant system 504 and machine learning system 508 may save data related to the transaction, for example, as part of transaction data 146, 240, or 300 and/or classification history data 241 (as will be discussed in further detail below). This is shown at dashed blocks 542 and 544. The transaction data and/or classification history data may be saved with one or more of the outputs of the machine learning system 508 (e.g., scalar fraud or anomaly probabilities) and the final results of the transaction (e.g., whether the transaction was approved or rejected). The saved data may be stored for use as training data for a machine learning model implemented by machine learning system 508 (e.g., as a basis for training data shown in one or more of fig. 8 and 10). The saved data may also be accessed as part of a future iteration of block 524, e.g., may form part of future assistance data. In some cases, the end result or outcome of the transaction may be unknown at the time of the transaction. For example, transactions may be marked as only abnormal via later review by an analyst and/or an automated system or based on feedback from the user (e.g., when the user reports fraud or indicates that the payment card or account was stolen from a certain date). In these cases, the ground truth labels may be collected over time after the transaction itself for the purpose of training the machine learning system 508.

Turning now to the alternative process flow of fig. 5B, in this case, one or more of the machine learning system 508 and the payment processor system 506 denies the transaction based on the output of the machine learning system 508. For example, if the scalar output of the machine learning system 508 is above the retrieved threshold, the transaction may be rejected. At block 552, the payment processor system 506 issues a response to the merchant system 504, which is received at block 554. At block 554, merchant system 504 takes steps to block the transaction from being completed and returns an appropriate response to POS or user device 502. The response is received at block 556 and the end user or customer may be informed that their payment has been denied, for example, via an on-screen "decline" message. The end user or customer may be prompted to use a different payment method. Although not shown in fig. 5B, in some cases, the issuing bank system 510 may be notified that a transaction associated with a particular account holder has been declined. The issuing bank system 510 may be caused to be notified as part of the process shown in fig. 5B, or may be notified as part of a periodic (e.g., daily) update. Although the transaction may not be part of the transaction data 146, 240, or 300 (because it is not approved), it may still be recorded by at least the machine learning system 508, as indicated by block 544. For example, for fig. 5A, the transaction data may be saved along with the output of the machine learning system 508 (e.g., scalar fraud or anomaly probabilities) and the final result of the transaction (e.g., the transaction was rejected).

Machine learning system with classification history module

Some examples described herein (such as machine learning systems 160, 210, 402, and 508 in fig. 1A-1C, 2A and 2B, 4, and 5A and 5B) may be implemented as a modular platform that allows for the use of different machine learning models and configurations to provide the transaction processing described herein. As technology improves and/or based on specific features of available data, the modular platform may allow for the use of different machine learning models and configurations.

A machine learning system 600 in accordance with an embodiment of the present invention is shown in fig. 6 and 7, as described in further detail below.

As previously discussed, it should be noted that although in the particular embodiments described below, the state data is stored in a vector table, the state data may be readily structured as n-dimensional tensors and/or may be stored in some other data structure or format, for example, in a multi-dimensional array. Similarly, the various vectors described with respect to this embodiment (e.g., input vector, output vector, etc.) may also be n-dimensional tensors, and may be stored using any suitable data structure.

The machine learning system 600 receives input data 601 and maps it to scalar outputs 602. This general process follows the same framework as previously described. The machine learning system 600 includes a first processing stage (or "lower model") 603 and a second processing stage (or "upper model") 604.

The machine learning system 600 is applied to data associated with at least the proposed transaction to generate a scalar output 602 for the proposed transaction. Scalar output 602 represents the likelihood that the proposed transaction presents a behavioral anomaly, e.g., the proposed transaction presents a different action or event pattern than expected or typical. In some cases, scalar output 602 represents the probability that the proposed transaction presents an anomaly in the sequence of actions, where the actions include at least the previous transaction for the entity and entity class pair, as outlined in more detail below. Scalar output 602 may be used to complete an approval decision for the proposed transaction, e.g., as described with reference to fig. 5A and 5B, may be used to decide whether to approve or reject the proposed transaction.

The input data may include transaction time data and transaction characteristic data. The transaction time data may include data derived from a time stamp such as that shown in fig. 3B or any other data format representing the date and/or time of the transaction. The date and/or time of the transaction may be set to the time the transaction was initiated at the client computing device, such as 110 or 502, or may be set to the time the request was received at the machine learning system 600, e.g., similar to the time the request was received at block 522 in fig. 5A and 5B. The transaction time data may include time data for a plurality of transactions, such as a historical set of the currently proposed transaction and one or more prior transactions. Time data for a historical set of one or more prior transactions may be received with the request and/or retrieved from a storage device communicatively coupled to the machine learning system 600.

In the arrangement of fig. 6, the transaction time data is converted into relative time data for application of one or more neural network architectures. In particular, the transaction time data is converted into a set of time differences, wherein the time differences represent the time difference Δt between the currently proposed transaction and the preceding transaction (typically the most recent preceding transaction). For example, the time difference may comprise a normalized time difference in seconds, minutes, or hours. The time difference Δt can be calculated by subtracting the time stamp of the previous transaction (or transactions, where multiple differences are being calculated and used) from the time stamp of the proposed transaction. The time difference value may be normalized by dividing by a maximum predefined time difference and/or clipping at the maximum time difference value.

In the inference mode, the machine learning system 600 detects feature sets from the input data 601 using an upper model 603 and a lower model 604 as outlined in more detail below. The output from the upper model 604 is a scalar value 602 that is used in determining whether to block the transaction (e.g., by comparing the scalar value 602 to a threshold).

As shown in fig. 6, the machine learning system 600 includes an embedded layer based on a feedforward neural network within the lower model 603. In this particular embodiment, the embedded layer is the first multi-layer perceptron 610, however it will be appreciated that this could alternatively be any other type of feed-forward neural network, such as a converter layer or a neural arithmetic logic unit.

The first multi-layer perceptron 610 includes a fully connected neural network architecture that includes multiple neural network layers (e.g., 1-10 layers) to pre-process data from the proposed transaction of input 601. Although a multi-layer perceptron is described herein, in some implementations, preprocessing may be omitted (e.g., if the received transaction data in the input data 601 is already in a suitable format) and/or only a single layer linear mapping may be provided. In some examples, preprocessing may be considered a form of "embedding" or "initial mapping" layer of the input transaction data. In some cases, one or more of the neural network layers of the first multi-layer perceptron 610 may provide for learning scaling and/or normalization of the received transaction data. In general, the fully connected neural network architecture of the first multi-layer perceptron 610 represents a first learning feature pre-processing stage that converts input data associated with the proposed transaction into feature vectors for further processing. In some cases, the fully connected neural network architecture may learn certain relationships, such as certain correlations, between elements of the transaction characteristic data and output an effective representation that accounts for these correlations. In one case, the input transaction data may include integer and/or floating point numbers, and the output 612 of the first multi-layer perceptron 610 may include a vector of values between 0 and 1. The number of elements or cells (i.e., the output vector size) of the first multi-layer sensor 610 may be set to a configurable super-parameter. In some cases, the number of elements or units may be between 32 and 2048.

The output 612 produced by the first multi-layer perceptron 610 is split into two portions 612a, 612b, which are provided to a time decay unit 614 and a classification history module 616, respectively. However, it will be appreciated that although these are shown as being entirely separable, arrangements are contemplated in which there is at least some overlap in the portion of the output 612 that is fed to each of the time decay unit 614 and the classification history module 616.

It should be noted that the input transaction data of input 601 may include data from the proposed transaction (e.g., as received via one or more of the client device, POS device, merchant server device, and payment processor server device) as well as data associated with the proposed transaction but not contained in the data packet associated with the proposed transaction. For example, as described with reference to fig. 1A-1C and fig. 2A and 2B, the input 601 may also include assistance data (such as 148 and 242), where the assistance data is retrieved by the machine learning system 600 (such as shown in fig. 1C) and/or by the payment processor server 140 (such as shown in fig. 1A or fig. 1B). The exact content included in the input data 601 may vary between implementations. This example relates to a general technical architecture for processing transaction data, rather than the exact form of the data. In general, since the machine learning system 600 includes a set of neural network layers, parameters may be learned based on any input data configuration desired or based on available input data. This example relates to engineering of such a technical architecture to enable transaction processing at the speeds and scales described herein.

In the example of fig. 6, the output of the first multi-layer sensor 610 is received by a time decay unit 614. The time decay unit 614 is configured to generate output data o t based on the previous state data h t-1, the time difference Δt, and the portion of the output 612a provided by the first multi-layer sensor 610. The time decay unit 614 may implement the techniques described in WO/2022/008130 and WO/2022/008131, each of WO/2022/008130 and WO/2022/008131 being incorporated herein by reference in its entirety.

The previous state data h t-1 is a vector of values corresponding to the state of the system from previous transactions. Those skilled in the art will appreciate that, typically, the previous state data h t-1 is stored in memory and provides a history of patterns of transactions that have occurred so far. The status data is stored for each primary entity (e.g., cardholder) and thus the status data for a given primary entity provides information about the primary entity's previous transaction chain.

The extent to which the historical state data should have an impact on decisions related to the proposed transaction may depend on the time difference Δt. Some of the state data may be less relevant in assessing whether the proposed transaction is abnormal or fraudulent if a long period of time has elapsed since the previous transaction. The time decay unit 614 applies a decay function to the previous state data h t-1 based on the time difference Δt.

Once the previous state data h t-1 has been attenuated based on the time difference Δt, the time attenuation unit 614 performs mapping to generate output data o t. The time decay unit 614 also stores the new state data h t in memory for the next transaction.

The mapping process performed by the time decay unit 614 may be based on machine learning. For example, the time decay unit 614 may use a neural network mapping (e.g., one or more parameterized functions) to map the previous state data h t-1 and the output 612a from the first multi-layer perceptron 610 to fixed-size vector outputs of predefined size. However, it will be appreciated that other methods may be used that do not require any such neural network or other machine learning techniques.

The portion 612b of the output from the first multi-layer perceptron 614 is input to a classification history module 616, and specifically used by an update layer 619. Unlike the time decay unit 614, which operates using a single state data vector for each entity, the classification history module 616 builds a table (e.g., a lookup table) of multiple states, one state for each secondary class with which a primary entity has interacted, as can be better appreciated with reference to FIG. 7.

In a typical fraud application, the primary entity represents a payer or account holder, while the secondary category may represent a beneficiary of funds, such as a merchant. However, it should be understood that the secondary category may be any classification field in the data. For example, it may be a number or date and time field that has been divided into different categories, e.g., the "quantity" may be divided into "low", "medium" and "high" categories, the date and time may be divided into hours of the day or days of the week, etc. The category may also be a combination of multiple categories (e.g., merchant identity linked to day of the week). The categories need not be ordered. Hereinafter, in this particular example, we refer to the secondary classification field as "merchant" for clarity. Note that all states will still be associated with the primary entity such that state data is stored and retrieved for a particular entity-class pair. It will be appreciated that, therefore, there will typically be a table of this kind for each primary entity.

In one exemplary software-based implementation, the table is a 2D tensor (merchant _state_size, max_num_ merchant _state) of the shape, whose columns represent the individual states of different merchants (it will of course be appreciated that different minor categories may be used in other examples). It will be appreciated that "max_num_ merchant _state" is the maximum number of merchants for which status data is stored (or equivalently, other category values such as day of the week, transaction amount or interval, etc.), i.e., the number of columns in the table. Meanwhile, "merchant _state_size" is the number of independent values stored in each column, i.e., the number of rows in the table. As mentioned above, it should be appreciated that typically for each primary entity (i.e., for each account holder) there will be a status data table such that the stored merchant (i.e., secondary category) data is specific to that primary entity.

The table in this example has a fixed size and thus it has a limit on the number of merchant states that can be stored. As input it receives the lookup table G t-1 (for that entity) from the previous time step t-1 and an update vector of size merchant state size. As an output, it returns a vector containing updated merchant status. In some implementations, the vector may also include the attenuated merchant state, for example by providing a vector of size 2 x merchant_state_size as a concatenation of the attenuated merchant state and the updated merchant state (for the current merchant).

As shown in fig. 7, for each transaction, classification history module 616 performs decay and update logic similar to standard time decay unit 614. The classification history module 616 first applies an exponential time decay to all stored states in the table G t-1, where the decay is based on the time difference Δt since the last transaction.

The decay function enables the selective and regulated use of previous transaction data (that is, it may apply a certain degree of "forgetting") based on the time difference Δt between the proposed transaction and the previous transaction, wherein the previous transaction data is an aggregate function of the transaction feature vectors of a plurality of previous transactions.

The decay function may be applied as a form of a vectorized exponential time decay function, of the form f(s) = [ e [-s/w_1],e[-s/w_2],……,e[-s/w_d] ], i.e., as a series of parameterized time decay calculations, wherein [ w_1, w_2..the..w_d ] includes in seconds: units represent a set of weights for "decay length", and where d is the size of the recursive state vector (which may typically be equal to the length of the state data vector operated on by the decay function). In this case Δt is passed to the function as s to output a vector of length d, for example Δt may be passed as a scalar floating point value representing the number of seconds elapsed between a previous event (e.g. transaction) and a current event (e.g. proposed transaction) of the same entity. The decay factors (i.e., weights) may be learned during the training process.

The decay weights may be fixed (e.g., manually configurable) parameters and/or may include trainable parameters. In the case of an exponential function, the decay length may include (or be trained to include) a mix of different values representing decays from a few minutes to a few weeks, such that both short-term and long-term behavior are captured. The time decay function is applied to the state data table from the previous iteration using element-by-element multiplication (e.g., computing Hadamard products) between the time decay vector and each state data entry (state data stored for each category, i.e., column in the table). In this example, the state data includes a two-dimensional table of vectors, where each vector is the same length as the transaction characteristic vector output. This effectively controls how much of the state data from the previous iteration is remembered and how much is forgotten.

A series of time decay constants may be used to decay the table. For example, a short time scale decay will suppress memory contributions from old activities, while a long time scale decay will preserve memory contributions from old activities. This enables the network to compare old and new activities to determine novelty. Furthermore, the status update is a function of the input properties of the event. This means that some state elements may only be updated for certain types of events. This is graphically illustrated in fig. 7 by the grouping of the different rows in the table, with the top three rows being reserved for a relatively long period of time, the middle three rows being reserved for a medium period of time, and the bottom three rows being reserved for a relatively short period of time. However, it will be appreciated that this is merely an example, and that different time periods may be suitably applied to each portion of the state data.

The network may learn that only certain types of activities (e.g., low value transactions) with a given merchant were previously seen, and thus the current event is also novel, even though the merchant was previously. For example, when risk scoring a current high value activity, it may learn to ignore the existence of low value transactions with the merchant in the past. The actual attenuation applied may be learned or may be predetermined (and may be user-defined, for example, during initial setup or optimization of the system). In either case, the machine learning system may learn which decay weights should be applied to which combinations of behavioral characteristics.

While in this exemplary embodiment the entire table of a given entity is attenuated, other embodiments are contemplated in which only the currently selected column is attenuated. To achieve this, a timestamp may be stored for each entity-category pair, and the time difference Δt is taken as the time between the current transaction and the time at which the data of the most recent instance of that entity-category pair was stored in the table.

After the decay step, classification history module 616 extracts the merchant status column that matches the current merchant Id (merchantId) (or zero vector if it is a new merchant as outlined below). Classification history module 616 queries the lookup table using the current merchant Id to see if the table contains status data for the merchant (i.e., whether a column exists). If so, the stored status data for that merchant Id is retrieved from the table. Conversely, if it is not present in the table, a new "default" state (e.g., zero vector) may be added to the table.

The output portion 612b from the multi-layer perceptron 610 (which in turn derives from the input vector x t as outlined previously) is then used by the update layer 619 to update the state data (appropriately retrieved or new) and insert it back into the table. Although different approaches may be taken for the updating step (i.e., for the step performed by the updating layer 619), in one implementation, element-wise addition is used to add together the attenuation state data vector of the entity-class pair and the input vector from the first multi-layer perceptron 610 (i.e., the output portion 612 b). This produces an output vector y t.

The tables are managed as a stack-updated columns are inserted in front of the tables, and the least recently updated columns are located behind the tables. Due to the size limitation of the table, if the table is full, a new merchant status will be added by discarding the least recently seen merchant status. As can be seen in fig. 7, the updated status data for the transaction is inserted in front of the table and the "gap" (shown in dashed lines) left behind is closed.

The outputs o t、yt of the time decay unit 614 and the classification history module 616 are received by the upper model 604, and in particular by the second feedforward neural network output layer. In this particular embodiment, the output layer is the second multilayer perceptron 620, however it will be appreciated that this could alternatively be any other type of feed forward neural network, such as a converter layer or a neural arithmetic logic unit. In this particular embodiment, the input data 601 is also fed to the second multi-layer sensor 620. In this example, the outputs o t、yt of the time decay unit 614 and the classification history module 616 are passed directly to the second multi-layer perceptron 620. However, other embodiments (not shown) are contemplated in which the transfer is accomplished indirectly via one or more additional intermediate neural network layers.

A second multi-layer perceptron 620 is used to generate scalar output 602. The second multi-layer perceptron 620 comprises a fully-connected neural network architecture, which in turn comprises a plurality of neural network layers, for receiving the outputs o t、yt of the time decay unit 614 and the classification history module 616, and the input data 601, and mapping those outputs o t、yt to scalar values 602. This may include a series of dimension reduction layers. The last activation function in the plurality of neural network layers may include a sigmoid activation function for mapping the output to a range of 0 to 1. The second multi-layer perceptron 620 may be trained to extract correlations between features output by the attention mechanisms (e.g., which may use multiple attention heads in a manner known per se in the art) and apply one or more nonlinear functions to ultimately output the scalar values 602.

The scalar value 602 may then be used by another portion of the transaction processing pipeline (not shown) in deciding whether the transaction should be allowed to continue normally or whether the transaction should be stopped and marked as fraudulent or anomalous. For example, the system may compare the scalar value 602 to an appropriate threshold such that a score exceeding the threshold is marked as abnormal.

In a preferred implementation, the status data is physically relevant, i.e., specific to a particular user, account holder, or merchant account. In this way, an appropriate entity may be identified as part of transaction data preprocessing, and the machine learning system 600 may be configured for that entity. In one case, the machine learning system 600 may apply the same parameters to the neural network architecture of each entity, but may store the state data separately, and may retrieve only historical transaction data and/or assistance data associated with (e.g., indexed by) the entity. Thus, the machine learning system 600 may include entity state storage, e.g., as described with reference to fig. 2A and 2B, whereby data of different entities may be efficiently partitioned. In other cases, the parameters of the decay function may be shared across multiple entities. This may be advantageous to reduce the number of learnable parameters for each entity of the overall machine learning system. For example, the exponential time decay weights described above may be fixed (or learned) and shared across multiple entities, while the state data may be unique to each entity.

Training machine learning system for processing transaction data

In some examples, the labeled training data may be used to train a machine learning system (such as the machine learning systems described herein). For example, a training set may be provided that includes data associated with transactions that have been marked as "normal" or "fraudulent. In one case, these tags may be provided based on reported fraudulent activity, i.e., using past fraud reports. For example, data associated with transactions that have been approved and processed without subsequent fraud reporting may be marked as "0" or "normal", while data associated with transactions that have been rejected and/or transactions that have been later reported as fraudulent and otherwise marked or blocked may be marked as "1" or abnormal.

An end-to-end training process may be performed so that the machine learning system may learn appropriate values for any and all of the learnable parameters. This may for example comprise training parameters of any multi-layer perceptron and/or attenuation weights for the attenuation function. It will be appreciated that any suitable training algorithm known per se in the art may be used and that the principles of the present invention are not limited to any particular training algorithm. However, by way of example, a suitable training algorithm may be based on random gradient descent, and may use back propagation of errors in model predictions to iteratively refine model parameters in order to find model parameters that minimize the objective function. In one case, the objective function (which measures the error in model prediction) may be defined as the binary cross entropy between the predicted value 602 and the ground truth label ("0" or "1").

Those skilled in the art will appreciate that where reference is made to the respective rows and columns of the state data table, the respective roles of those rows and columns may be exchanged such that state data is stored in the rows indexed by the category identifiers and state data values of the respective features are stored in the columns.

It will be appreciated that embodiments of the present invention may provide an arrangement in which the classification history module brings signal extraction from interaction monitoring into the architecture. Advantageously, this may lead to an improvement in speed and/or confidentiality of the implementation. In particular, the data scientists no longer need to manually design features of this type, meaning that they do not need to be disclosed as input to a classifier for model management, and the implementation time of the model is reduced.

In addition, embodiments of the present invention may provide improvements in detection performance. The classification history module may learn more subtle interaction logic than a human being would manually design in a limited time. In particular, the classification history module may learn patterns of user activity specific to each category and detect anomalies based on historical data of related entity-category pairs. This method may provide a significant detection enhancement over other methods known per se in the art.
